title: Naturalistic Short-term Associations Between Automatic Thoughts, Irrational Beliefs, and Depressive Symptom Severity During Initial SSRI Treatment in Major Depressive Disorder
abstract: Cognitive models of depression distinguish between proximal automatic thoughts and broader irrational belief systems. However, little is known about how these cognitive contents co-vary with depressive symptoms during the early phase of pharmacological treatment under naturalistic conditions. This study examined short-term associations between automatic thoughts (ATs), irrational beliefs (IBs), and depressive symptom severity during the first four weeks of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) initiation. Forty-four outpatients meeting DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder were assessed at baseline and after four weeks of SSRI treatment. Measures included the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire (ATQ), and Irrational Beliefs Scale (ABS-2). Hierarchical regression analyses examined cross-sectional and change-score associations. Effect sizes (f²) and 95% confidence intervals were reported. Automatic thoughts demonstrated strong cross-sectional associations with depressive severity at baseline (R² = .598, f² = 1.49) and week four (R² = .774, f² = 3.42). Irrational beliefs showed moderate associations (R² = .37, f² = .59). In hierarchical models, ATQ scores accounted for substantial incremental variance beyond irrational beliefs (ΔR² range: .21–.34). Change-score analyses indicated strong concurrent covariation between reductions in automatic thoughts and symptom improvement. Findings suggest that proximal cognitive content (automatic thoughts) closely tracks depressive symptom severity during SSRI treatment under naturalistic conditions. Results should not be interpreted as causal or predictive but rather as descriptive of concurrent cognitive–symptom dynamics. Controlled longitudinal designs are required to evaluate temporal precedence.
